The reading reverses the claim that performing a unit's technique instills the unit's values, arguing from analysts' transfers out of toxicology into narcotics that preexisting personal preferences selected who stayed in or left each technique (pp. 626, 630, 632).

The reading keeps the contrast in occupational cultures between toxicology and narcotics but attributes it partly to organizational hiring and transfer arrangements through which employees sorted themselves into tasks they already preferred (pp. 613, 619, 630).

The reading keeps all three unit outcomes at MCCL but explains them solely by whether an analyst faced an impending personal challenge in the local court, treating occupational values as post-hoc descriptions that cannot be separated from local exposure in a single-lab design (pp. 624–625, 632, 635).

The reading replaces enduring differences in occupational values with a shared practical rule across units in which analysts revise established practices when a credible local challenge threatens their ability to testify and defend existing work when no immediate local consequence looms (pp. 624, 627, 632).

The reading keeps narcotics analysts' retention of crystal testing but explains it as a defense of throughput capacity under short statutory charging clocks and a two-instrument bottleneck rather than a refusal grounded primarily in craft values (pp. 629, 631–632).

The reading takes the narcotics passages on expected shifts to GC/MS, ongoing working-group debates, camera pricing, capacity bottlenecks, and a Daubert hearing workshop and reads them as an unfinished snapshot of anticipated compliance and capacity limits at the close of fieldwork rather than settled resistance (pp. 629, 631–633, 635).
